children: By Kevin Elliott

My wife, Camille, and I are no strangers to life overseas. We have spent a little more than seven years as expats, most of it in Doha, Qatar, where I worked as an engineer. But when my contract expired earlier this year, we decided not to return to the U.S. and instead start a new chapter abroad: retiring in Hua Hin, Thailand.

Not surprisingly, living overseas as retirees is a different experience from doing so while collecting a paycheck. We've also discovered that not everything goes as planned, and that it takes patience to adapt to a new culture.
But are we glad we made the move? No question about it.
Affordable on Social Security

When we were first looking for a potential retirement destination, we watched a lot of YouTube videos and saw many promoting how affordable Hua Hin would be. They made it seem possible for a couple to enjoy a comfortable retirement on $2,000 to $2,500 a month.

Those estimates turned out to be misleading, at best. It costs a lot to set up a house, to run air conditioning in a tropical climate and buy imported foods and eat at Western restaurants. Nearly a year into our expat life, we're finding that $3,000 to $3,500 a month is a more realistic number for a couple, and probably about half that for someone who is single.
Still, that lets us live here comfortably on our Social Security benefits.

What's more, some things are relative bargains compared with living in a major city overseas or returning to the U.S. We pay $870 a month for a two-level, three-bedroom, 21/2-bath house with a large yard for our four small dogs.

And while Western restaurants can be costly, a couple can eat dinner for just $8 to $20 at a local restaurant, or a bit less for breakfast. (Another savings: Tips aren't expected as they are in the U.S., but if the service and food are good, we tip a little bit.)
Healthcare considerations

Healthcare options are plentiful and the costs are reasonable. Our health insurance costs about $3,000 a year for good inpatient coverage for both of us, and outpatient care is affordable enough that we pay out of pocket.

Finding doctors and specialists has been relatively easy. Hua Hin has English-speaking physicians and specialists in areas such as cardiology, orthopaedics, neurology and gastroenterology. At Bangkok Hospital Hua Hin, current checkup packages start around $95. A gastroscopy or colonoscopy package starts around $500. Mammogram and breast ultrasound packages can run roughly $60 to $100.

Getting around locally and traveling farther afield also are reasonably priced. We can fly from Bangkok — which is about 21/2 to four hours away from Hua Hin, depending on the mode of transportation and traffic — to other parts of Southeast Asia for less than $600 round trip for two. Round-trip tickets to the U.S. typically cost a total of around $2,000 to $2,500 for both of us.

While a car isn't a must-have, we and other expats do tend to buy or rent for convenience as the public-transportation system is limited to pickup trucks converted into shared buses, and taxi service can be unreliable farther out from central Hua Hin. But car ownership isn't complicated or expensive. The steps to obtaining a Thai license are about the same as in the U.S. — proof of residence and insurance, for instance — and the costs for insurance range from about $300 to $600 a year. A major car repair costs between $200 and $300.
Living like a local

Getting our visas was relatively straightforward. Americans aged 50 and older can apply for a retirement visa, generally by showing they have at least 800,000 baht (about $24,000) in a Thai bank account or meeting certain income requirements. The process typically involves obtaining an initial visa and then applying for a one-year extension, which can be renewed annually. Retirees must also report their address to immigration authorities every 90 days, unless they reset the clock by traveling out of country.

Once the setup phase ended, real life started. Expat life is about new relationships and building a community, and both have been surprisingly easy for us in Hua Hin. We've met several expats here in Hua Hin and do dinner and events regularly.
Depending on where you live in Hua Hin, you may experience tropical animal life. We've had lizards, too many frogs to count, a small python and a turtle in our backyard.
The surprises
What's been the toughest part of our time here? First, the language barrier. Neither of us speaks much Thai, so we rely on the Google Translate app to manage everyday tasks.
Next would be the heat and humidity, which can be overwhelming most of the time. Hua Hin feels a lot like a Florida summer for much of the year, but without Florida's cooler winter months.

Then there are phone calls home to family and friends. When you're 11 hours ahead of the Eastern U.S., it's hard to stay in touch consistently. Family and friends struggle with when to call us, which means fewer calls than we'd like.

Crime isn't a major concern of ours. There have been a few petty thefts reported in local news, but Hua Hin is safe. I've been told by several expats who have lived here for a while that the presence of the Thai royal family, who summer in Hua Hin, keeps the city extra safe and crime rate lower than other destination cities.

There have been happy surprises, too. As Black expats, we've felt welcome. While the country has its cultural differences, we haven't encountered the issues related to racial prejudices found too often in the U.S.

We've also been struck by the kindness and honesty of people we've met. Some service providers will charge more to foreigners than locals — for instance, we paid a handyman 1,500 baht for two to three hours of work, then learned that the average wage for a skilled worker is 400 to 500 baht a day. But those experiences have been overshadowed by the good. A Thai fisherman found an iPhone we lost in the water at a marina, and a lost wallet came back with all the money and credit cards still in it.
Final thoughts

What would I say to someone in their 60s who is thinking about retiring in Thailand? First, it isn't for everyone. You need a sense of adventure, an openness to different cultures and a willingness to endure the tough moments of expat life, because they will happen more than you expect.

But if you budget in local terms, give yourself at least six months before you judge whether you've made the right move, and find activities that get you out of the house, retiring in Thailand can be rewarding.

Ultimately, when people ask whether we'd ever move back to the U.S., Camille points out that we couldn't afford the lifestyle we've created here elsewhere. While she could do without the relentless heat and humidity — especially what it does to her hair — she's discovered that what makes retirement here worthwhile has as much to do with the life we've created as the money we've saved.
